name: Adlay seed extract

card.summary: Adlay seed extract comes from Job's tears (Coix lacryma-jobi), a grain used in traditional Asian medicine and marketed in skincare as a brightening botanical.
card.aka: Coix seed extract; Job's tears extract; yi yi ren
card.note: Published human work concerns oral coix seed, not topical brightening.

quick.overview:
Adlay is the seed of Coix lacryma-jobi, a tall grass native to Southeast Asia, also sold as Chinese pearl barley. In traditional Chinese medicine the polished seed is called yi yi ren. Skincare products use its extract as a brightening botanical aimed at a more even-looking complexion.
Research on coix seed is mostly oral and laboratory work on metabolism, gut microbiota and immune function; a review noted effects such as hypoglycaemic and anti-inflammatory activity. A small human trial in healthy men looked at gut microbiota and lymphocytes.
quick.how: It appears as an ingredient in cosmetic serums and creams and as a food grain or herbal preparation.
quick.risks: It is a food and traditional medicine ingredient; a 2023 study reported mycotoxin screening of medicinal foods as a quality topic.

lead: Adlay (Coix lacryma-jobi), also called Job's tears, is a grass native to Southeast Asia whose seeds are sold as Chinese pearl barley and, in traditional Chinese medicine, as yi yi ren.[1]
Extracts are marketed in skincare as brightening botanicals. Wikipedia's article does not discuss cosmetic or skin-lightening uses; it cites a Kampo study on coix-containing formulas for warts.[1]
Published research centres on the seed as food and medicine, with reviews describing hypoglycaemic, liver, anti-tumour, gut microbiota and anti-inflammatory effects.[2][3]

chain: Marketed to even out skin tone
angle.text: Skincare brands use adlay extract as a brightening ingredient. People apply it hoping for a more even tone; the human studies found so far concern eating the seed, not topical lightening.

paras: The polished seeds, yi yi ren, are used in traditional Chinese medicine, often with other herbs. The seed is roughly 65% carbohydrate, 14% protein and 5% fat.[1]

A 2024 review covered traditional usage, chemical components and pharmacology of coix seed.[2] A 2026 review covered nutrition, functional properties and food products.[3] A 2023 review addressed anti-tumour effects.[4]

A randomised trial in healthy male adults examined how coix seed consumption affects gut microbiota and peripheral lymphocyte subsets; its introduction notes that coix seed has been suggested to promote regression of viral skin infection.[5] No studies found on topical skin brightening.
